items.title: UN condemns Trump threats to bomb Iran civilian infrastructure

featured_image.name: UN Flags Legal Risks as Trump Threatens Strikes on Iran Civilian Targets -  Bloomberg

items.description:
The United Nations on Monday warned the United States that any strikes on Iranian civilian infrastructure would constitute a clear violation of international law, responding to President Donald Trump's escalating threats to destroy Iran's power plants and bridges if Tehran does not reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

"We were alarmed by the rhetoric seen in that social media post that threatened American attacks on power plants, bridges, and other infrastructure should Iran not agree to a deal," Stephane Dujarric, chief spokesman for UN Secretary-General António Guterres, said at a daily briefing on Monday. "Any attack on civilian infrastructure is a violation of international law, and a very clear one."[1]

items.title: Cambridge solar reactor turns plastic waste into hydrogen

featured_image.name: Solar reactor uses old battery acid to turn plastic waste into clean  hydrogen

items.description: Researchers at the University of Cambridge have developed a solar-powered reactor that uses acid recovered from spent car batteries to break down hard-to-recycle plastics into clean hydrogen fuel and valuable industrial chemicals. The results, published in the journal Joule, describe a process the team calls "solar-powered acid photoreforming" that could offer a cheaper, more sustainable path for dealing with plastic waste.[1][2]

items.title: Artemis II breaks Apollo 13's distance record during lunar flyby

featured_image.name: Artemis II lunar mission goals, explained | Popular Science

items.description:
Four astronauts aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft shattered a 56-year-old record on Monday afternoon, traveling farther from Earth than any humans in history. At 1:56 p.m. EDT on April 6, 2026, the Artemis II crew surpassed the 248,655-mile mark set by Apollo 13 in April 1970, ultimately reaching a maximum distance of approximately 252,757 miles from Earth — more than 4,100 miles beyond the previous record.[1][2][3]

The crew — Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, Mission Specialist Christina Koch, and Canadian Space Agency Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen — became the first humans to visit the moon's vicinity since Apollo 17 in December 1972.[4][3]

items.title: NY Fed: Supply chain stress hit three-year high in March

featured_image.name: High stakes in the Strait of Hormuz: Force majeure and supply chain ...

items.description:
Global supply chain pressures intensified in March, reaching their highest point in more than three years, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported Monday in its latest Global Supply Chain Pressure Index release.

The GSCPI rose to 0.68 in March, up from a revised 0.54 in February, according to the data published by the New York Fed. A reading of zero represents normal supply chain conditions, while positive values indicate above-average strain. The March figure marks the index's highest level since early 2023, when pandemic-era disruptions were still unwinding.[1][2]

items.title: OpenAI CFO questions Altman's push for late 2026 IPO

featured_image.name: OpenAI hires former Nextdoor CEO Sarah Friar as first CFO ...

items.description:
A rift has emerged at the top of OpenAI over the timing and affordability of what could become one of the largest public listings in technology history. Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar has privately questioned CEO Sam Altman's push to take the company public as early as the fourth quarter of 2026, warning that OpenAI may not be organizationally prepared for such a move, according to a report by The Information published Saturday.[1]

Friar has also raised concerns about Altman's commitment to spend $600 billion on computing infrastructure over the next five years, citing doubts about whether the company's revenue trajectory can support purchases of that magnitude. The tensions between the two most senior figures overseeing OpenAI's finances and strategy represent an unusual public signal of internal friction at the world's most valuable startup.[2][3]
